docs.title: One login for all your division's services
docs.text:
Handover is an OAuth2 provider that sits between VATSIM Connect and your division's websites. Members log in once through Handover, and your services use Handover instead of talking to VATSIM Connect directly.

  • Install it in production

    Run Handover as a container next to your MySQL database

    Installation

  • Keep member data in one place

    Members accept your Data Protection Policy once, and you scrub data from one system

    Data protection policy

  • Connect your services

    Any OAuth2 client that supports VATSIM Connect can use Handover with the same scopes and user data

    Connecting a client

  • Manage groups

    Assign members to groups, delegate who manages them, and share memberships with your services

    Groups

  • Open Source, GPL

    Handover is licensed under the GPL-3.0 and freely available on GitHub

    Licence

  • Make it better

    Help by contributing to Handover itself

    Contribute

Handover was created by Daniel L. (1352906) and Matan B. (1375048). Special thanks to VATSIM UK, whose open source core system helped us on the right track.

docs.title: Contribute
docs.text: Contributions help everyone move Handover forward with fixes and features. Fork the repository on GitHub, so you can open pull requests back to the main project.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Name branches feat/name-here for features and fix/name-here for fixes, for example feat/new-api or fix/login-bug.
  • The service language is UK English. This applies to the interface and to this documentation. Keep established technical terms as they are, such as the OAuth "authorization code" grant.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
This site is built with MkDocs and Material for MkDocs, and versioned with mike. The sources live in the docs/ folder, and CI publishes them to the gh-pages branch.

Install PDM, for example the version pinned in mise.toml with mise install, then install the dependencies:

cd docs
pdm install

docs.title: Live preview
docs.text:
For quick edits, serve the current sources with live reload on localhost:8000:

pdm run docs:live

docs.title: Versioned preview
docs.text:
To see the site as it is published, with the version selector, use two terminals in the docs/ folder. In the first, start mike's server on localhost:8000/dev/:

pdm run docs:serve

In the second, build the dev version into your local gh-pages branch:

pdm run docs:build

Re-run pdm run docs:build after each change. It only updates /dev/, and it never pushes.

docs.title: Check before you push
docs.text:
CI builds the site in strict mode, which fails on any warning. Run the same check locally:

pdm run docs:check

The output goes to docs_site/, which is ignored.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: The groups system is a general-purpose membership and delegation layer. Administrators define named groups, assign users to them, and write rules that let certain groups manage the membership of others. Client applications can request the groups OAuth scope to receive a user's group memberships via GET /api/user.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A group has a slug, an optional description, tags, and attribute values. Tags are free-form strings; attributes are key/value pairs drawn from a global schema of attribute definitions (e.g. region, division). Any number of groups can be marked as admin groups. Members of those groups have full system access.

Manager rules control delegation. A rule says that members of one group (the manager group) can manage the membership of other groups. Rules can match by a specific target group, by tag (any group carrying a given tag), or by attribute value (any group whose attribute matches a key/value pair). Tag and attribute rules are global: they match every group that satisfies the pattern, including ones created in the future.

Manager access is resolved at request time by checking whether any rule points at the requested group through the user's own memberships. The result is cached per user with a 5-minute TTL and invalidated whenever memberships or rules change.

docs.title: Member groups (transitive membership)
docs.text:
A group can be a member of another group. When group C is a member of group P, every member of C also counts as a member of P, and of every group P is a member of. A group can be a member of several groups. A change that would make a group a member of itself, directly or through other groups, is rejected.

A group's members page lists its Member groups: the groups that are members of it. The group's own page lists Member of: the groups it is a member of, directly and through those groups. An indirect entry names the direct group it comes through. Internally these are child and parent edges in the group_hierarchy table.

Inherited membership is reflected in two places:

  • The groups API array lists inherited groups alongside direct ones, each tagged with a direct boolean (false for inherited).
  • Manager rules match on a user's effective group set, so managing rights held by a group flow down to everyone in its member groups.

Membership through another group deliberately does not grant admin: a user in a member group of an admin group is not an administrator. Admin access is always a direct membership.

System administrators edit member groups on the members page, and Member of on the group page with the Edit toggle on. Only direct entries can be removed.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
There are three access levels. System administrators (members of any is_admin_group group) have full CRUD over groups, memberships, rules, and attribute definitions. Group managers can add and remove members of the groups their rules cover, but cannot edit group metadata or rules. Everyone else can view their own memberships via the API.

The web interface lives under /groups. Managers see only the groups they can manage; admins see everything. A global rules overview at /groups/rules shows every delegation rule across all groups in one place.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Requesting the groups scope adds a groups array to the /api/user response. Each entry carries the group's id, slug, name, tags, attributes, and whether the membership is direct. See the user API for the response shape and the stability of each field.

docs.title: Use-cases
docs.text:
To gate access in a client application, create a group, add members, and check groups[*].id in the API response. No hard-coded roles required.

To stop everyone outside a group from signing in to a client at all, make the group one of the client's required groups. You cannot delete a group while a client requires it.

To delegate roster management without granting full admin access, create a group for the managers (e.g. "vACC Directors") and a tag-match rule granting it management of every group tagged vacc. Any future group with that tag is automatically covered.

To manage a whole region or division uniformly, assign a shared attribute (e.g. region = EUR) to the relevant groups and write one attribute-match rule. The managing group gains access to all matching groups past and future.

Manager rules can be mutual or self-referential, which supports federated governance patterns where groups co-administer each other.

To bootstrap the first administrator, run php artisan groups:add-admin {cid}. This finds or creates a system-administrators admin group and adds the user to it. See artisan commands.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Handover ships as a pre-built container image. We recommend running it with Docker, for example through Portainer.

docs.title: Docker (recommended)
docs.text:
• A Docker environment to run containers.
  • A MySQL database. The image does not include one.
  • A reverse proxy, if you host more than one website on the same server.
  • An OAuth client from VATSIM Connect.

docs.title: Manual (unsupported)
docs.text:
• A web server that can host PHP websites, such as Apache or Nginx.
  • A MySQL database.
  • PHP and extensions that meet the Laravel 13 requirements. Handover needs PHP 8.3 or newer.
  • You build the Composer and npm dependencies yourself, set up the scheduler, and clear caches on every update.

The commands on this site assume your container is named handover. Replace the name if yours differs.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Pull the ghcr.io/vatsim-scandinavia/handover:v4 image.
  2. Create the MySQL database.

  3. Create a volume for the storage folder. It holds sessions and the OAuth signing keys, so they survive when you recreate the container.

    docker volume create handover_storage

  4. Configure the environment variables. The repository's docker-compose.yaml is a good starting point.

  5. Start the container with the volume bound to /app/storage. On the first start, the container generates the OAuth signing key. If APP_KEY is empty, it also generates an application key.

  6. Read the generated application key and set it as the APP_KEY environment variable. Without a fixed key, users must log in again each time you recreate the container.

    docker exec -it handover php artisan key:get

  7. Create the database tables.

    docker exec -it --user www-data handover php artisan migrate

  8. Add a crontab entry outside the container that runs the scheduler every minute. See background jobs for what it runs.

    * * * * * docker exec --user www-data -i handover php artisan schedule:run >/dev/null

  9. Point your reverse proxy at port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS) in the container. The example docker-compose.yaml maps these to 8080 and 8443 on the host. The container creates a self-signed certificate for HTTPS on first start.

  10. Make yourself an administrator. Log in once, then run:

    docker exec -it --user www-data handover php artisan groups:add-admin YOUR_CID

You can now add OAuth clients and customise the theme.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
The image enables OPcache with production settings. PHP does not check files for changes, so restart the container after you change a file in it.

For development, set opcache.validate_timestamps to 1 in /usr/local/etc/php/php.ini. PHP then picks up changed files on its own.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Recreate the container with the new image, then apply database changes:

docker exec -it --user www-data handover php artisan migrate

Some releases need manual steps. Read the upgrade guide before you update.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
These are the operational steps for moving Handover between versions. Always read the section for your target version first. Some releases need manual steps.

Executing commands in containers

If you're using a container you need to execute the command inside of the container. For example, if you're using Docker you must prefix the command with docker exec and specify the container name. Here's an example where we assume that the container is handover:

docker exec -it --user www-data handover COMMAND [ARGUMENTS...]

docs.title: Before you upgrade
docs.text:
• Back up the database, plus the storage volume. The volume holds the OAuth signing keys in oauth-keys/. In 3.x, it held them in oauth-private.key and oauth-public.key. Losing the keys invalidates every access token already issued.
  • Rehearse on staging with a copy of production data when a release has breaking changes.
  • Note the image tag you run now, and keep the backup until the new version is confirmed healthy.

  • Put Handover in maintenance mode for the duration of the upgrade. The flag lives on the storage volume, so it survives recreating the container:

    php artisan down
# ... perform the upgrade ...
php artisan up

docs.title: All versions
docs.text:
Pull the new image and recreate the container. The image ships with Composer dependencies installed and frontend assets built, so you do not build anything yourself.

Then apply database changes and clear caches:

php artisan migrate --force
php artisan optimize:clear

If you run a custom theme, rebuild your custom image on the new version.

Why --force

In production, migrate asks for confirmation. Without an interactive terminal it answers no and does nothing. --force skips the prompt.

docs.title: Upgrading from 3.x to 4.0.0
docs.text:
This release moves Handover to Laravel 13 and Laravel Passport 13, and the frontend toolchain to Vite 8 and jQuery 4. It needs one manual step on the database: hashing the OAuth client secrets. The container also moves the OAuth signing key into a key store that supports key rotation. You need to do nothing for that.

OAuth breaks until you hash the client secrets

Every integration fails to get a token at /oauth/token until you run php artisan passport:hash. Members cannot log in to any connected service in the meantime. Plan the upgrade so you run it straight after the migration.

Access tokens now expire after one hour

After the upgrade, access tokens expire after one hour and refresh tokens expire after 30 days. If an integration uses an access token for more than an hour, it must use its refresh token to get a new one. If an integration does not refresh within 30 days, the member must sign in again. For details, see token lifetimes are shorter.

docs.title: Upgrade steps
docs.text:
1. Back up the database and the storage volume. This is not optional for this release: hashing the secrets, changing the client schema and moving the signing key cannot be undone, and a rollback needs the backup.

  2. Enable maintenance mode in the running 3.x container:

    php artisan down

  3. Change the image tag from :v3 to :v4, pull it, and recreate the container. The floating :v3 tag never moves to 4.0.0, so you must change it. On start, the container imports oauth-private.key into oauth-keys/. For details, see signing keys move to a key store.

  4. Apply the database changes:

    php artisan migrate --force

    The migrations do the following:

    • Add the group_hierarchy table for member groups.
    • Shorten the lifetime of existing refresh tokens.
    • Move OAuth clients to the Passport 13 client schema.
    • Give every client allowed scopes, required groups and a session setting.
    • Add the columns that OpenID Connect sign-ins need.
    • Add the allowed origins of public clients.
    • Add post-logout redirect URIs for logout.

    If you run Handover without the container, step 3 imports nothing, and the migration imports the signing key instead.

  5. Hash the OAuth client secrets. Run this once per environment:

    php artisan passport:hash --force

    Like migrate, the command asks for confirmation and answers no without an interactive terminal. --force skips the prompt. Running it twice is safe: it skips secrets that are already hashed.

  6. Clear the caches:

    php artisan optimize:clear

  7. Remove any VITE_THEME_* variables. They are no longer used. If you had custom colours, see light and dark themes.

  8. Lift maintenance mode:

    php artisan up

  9. Log in to a connected service through Handover. This confirms that the token exchange works with hashed secrets.

Warning

Never run passport:hash in CI or tests. It rewrites stored secrets.

docs.title: Rolling back to 3.x
docs.text:
Once you have run passport:hash, a 3.x container cannot verify any client secret, because 3.x compares secrets in plain text. Switching the image back is not enough.

  1. Switch the image tag back to the one you noted before the upgrade, and recreate the container.
  2. Restore the database backup you took in step 1.
  3. Restore oauth-private.key and oauth-public.key from the storage volume backup you took in step 1. 4.0.0 moved the signing key into oauth-keys/, and 3.x reads only these two files. If you set the key in PASSPORT_PRIVATE_KEY and PASSPORT_PUBLIC_KEY instead, set both variables again.
  4. Clear the caches with php artisan optimize:clear.

The group_hierarchy table from 4.0.0 does no harm to 3.x if you keep it, but the restore removes it anyway.

3.x cannot read the 4.0.0 client schema, so you must restore the backup. The restore removes every client created after the upgrade, together with its tokens. Clients created after the upgrade have UUID IDs, which 3.x cannot store. To keep such a client, create it again in 3.x and give the service its new ID and secret.

docs.title: Client secrets are hashed
docs.text:
Passport 13 hashes client secrets by default. 3.x stored them in plain text, which is why the manual passport:hash step exists.

Client owners change nothing. They keep sending their existing secret, and Passport hashes the incoming value to compare it. Clients you create after the upgrade are hashed from the start. Handover shows a new client's secret only once, so copy it when you create the client.

docs.title: OAuth clients are managed in the admin UI
docs.text:
Administrators now create, edit and delete clients, and regenerate their secrets, under OAuth Clients in the admin header. See OAuth clients.

Passport's JSON routes are gone: /oauth/clients, /oauth/scopes, /oauth/tokens and /oauth/personal-access-tokens. If you scripted against them, use the admin UI or the artisan commands instead. The routes your integrations use, /oauth/authorize, /oauth/token and /api/user, are unchanged.

docs.title: Token lifetimes are shorter
docs.text:
Access tokens now expire after one hour instead of one month. Refresh tokens now expire after 30 days instead of 100 years. Each refresh returns a new refresh token that is valid for another 30 days. An integration that refreshes at least once every 30 days keeps its access.

Each member can have one session per client. When a member signs in again, Handover revokes their earlier access and refresh tokens for that client.

Access tokens issued before the upgrade keep their one-month expiry. The migration updates each existing refresh token as follows:

  • If its access token is revoked, the migration revokes the refresh token.
  • If its access token is missing or has no expiry, the refresh token expires 30 days after the migration runs.
  • Otherwise, the refresh token expires 30 days after its access token expires.

The migration never extends a refresh token's expiry.

docs.title: OAuth clients use the Passport 13 schema
docs.text:
Client IDs are now strings. Existing clients keep their numeric ID, such as 5, so existing integrations change nothing. New clients get a UUID as their ID.

Each client now stores its redirect URIs as a list and its grant types explicitly. The migration fills both from the old columns:

  • The redirect URIs come from the old comma-separated redirect column.
  • The grant types are exactly the ones Passport allowed the client before the upgrade. For a client created in the admin UI, these are authorization code, refresh token, client credentials, implicit and device code.

New clients get only authorization code and refresh token. Administrators can change the grant types and redirect URIs of any client in the admin UI. Editing a client in the admin UI no longer drops its extra redirect URIs. See OAuth clients.

After the backfill, the migration drops the old user_id, redirect, personal_access_client and password_client columns, and the oauth_personal_access_clients table. You take no action. To undo the change, restore your backup as described in rolling back to 3.x.

docs.title: Clients limit scopes, members and sessions
docs.text:
Each client now has three settings:

  • Allowed scopes: the scopes the client may request.
  • Required groups: the groups whose members may sign in.
  • Single session: whether each member keeps one session with the client.

The migration sets them so that every existing client keeps its behaviour. You need to do nothing:

  • The client may request every scope that 3.x has: full_name, email, vatsim_details, country and groups.
  • The client has no required groups, so every member may sign in.
  • Each member keeps a single session with the client.

A request for a scope the client does not allow now fails with the invalid_scope error. In 3.x, Handover granted any known scope to any client.

When you create a client in the admin UI, you must pick its allowed scopes.

docs.title: Handover supports OpenID Connect
docs.text:
Handover is now an OpenID Connect provider. It adds:

  • Discovery at /.well-known/openid-configuration.
  • ID tokens.
  • A UserInfo endpoint at /oauth/userinfo.

See OpenID Connect.

You need to do nothing. OpenID Connect is opt-in for each client: a service can use it only after an administrator ticks the new openid scope in the client's allowed scopes. No existing client gets openid or profile, so existing services keep working.

Access tokens that hold the groups scope now carry a groups claim with the IDs of the member's groups.

docs.title: Handover supports public clients
docs.text:
Administrators can now create public clients for services that run in the member's browser. A public client has no secret, must use PKCE with the S256 method, and calls the token and UserInfo endpoints from its allowed origins. See OAuth clients and public clients.

Existing clients that have a secret do not change. A client created before 4.0.0 without a secret is now a public client:

  • It must send a code challenge with the S256 method. Handover now refuses the plain method.
  • When you edit it, its redirect URIs must use https, or http on localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1], and it may keep only the authorization code and refresh token grant types.

The token and UserInfo endpoints now check the Origin header for public clients. A request with an Origin header that the public client does not allow fails with a 403 response. Confidential clients are not affected, even when their server sends an Origin header.

docs.title: Logging out asks for confirmation
docs.text:
Handover's logout button now sends a form to the new end session endpoint, /oauth/logout. Logout now also ends the whole Handover session and renews its CSRF token.

Links to the old /logout path still work, but they no longer log the member out at once. Handover now asks "Log out of Handover?", and the member must confirm. If a service links to /logout, members need one more click. To log members out without asking, the service can use RP-initiated logout instead.

Services can now log members out of Handover through OpenID Connect. The migration gives every existing client an empty list of post-logout redirect URIs, so you need to do nothing. To let a service send members back after logout, add its post-logout redirect URIs in the admin UI. See post-logout redirect URIs.

docs.title: Signing keys move to a key store
docs.text:
Handover now keeps its OAuth signing keys in oauth-keys/ on the storage volume, and you can rotate them with artisan commands. See signing keys.

  • On the first start of 4.0.0, the container imports oauth-private.key as the first active key and deletes oauth-private.key and oauth-public.key. If you set PASSPORT_PRIVATE_KEY instead, the container imports that key.
  • Handover then ignores PASSPORT_PRIVATE_KEY and PASSPORT_PUBLIC_KEY. Remove them.
  • New access tokens carry a kid header that names their key. Access tokens from 3.x have none, and keep working while the imported key is published.
  • Handover publishes its public keys at /.well-known/jwks.json.
  • passport:keys no longer has any effect.

Services that read /api/user need no changes.

Services that check tokens with a copy of the public key

Some services check access tokens themselves, with a copy of oauth-public.key. They keep working after the upgrade, but fail once you rotate the key. Before you rotate, move them to the JWKS. See verifying access tokens.

docs.title: The groups API reports inherited groups
docs.text: Each entry in the groups array now has a direct field. Once you nest groups, the array also lists groups a member inherits. Clients that only want direct memberships should filter on direct: true. See the user API.

docs.title: Light and dark themes
docs.text:
Handover now has a light and a dark theme, and follows the operating system by default. Signed-in members can switch between system, light and dark with the toggle next to their name. The choice is kept in the browser.

The VITE_THEME_* variables are gone, including VITE_THEME_BORDER_RADIUS. The 4.0.0 betas still read them, so this applies to them too. If you set custom colours with them, copy resources/sass/themes/_custom.scss.example to _custom.scss, move your colours into it, and rebuild. Use _light.scss and _dark.scss as a reference. See customising the theme, which also covers how to bake a custom theme into a container image.

APP_NAME no longer changes the name Handover shows. Page titles and headings always say Handover. Set the new APP_TAGLINE to describe your instance beneath the front page heading. Leave APP_NAME as it is: it still names the session cookie, so changing or removing it signs every member out once. A footer on every page says who runs your Handover and credits Handover to VATSIM Scandinavia. See front page heading.

docs.title: Why this is a major release
docs.text: Passport 13 changed behaviour Handover depends on as an OAuth provider. It became headless, so the authorization endpoint needs a view bound, and it switched client IDs to UUIDs. Handover handles both in code, and existing clients keep their numeric IDs. Hashing the client secrets cannot be handled in code, because it rewrites stored data. That manual step is what makes this 4.0.0 rather than a 3.x release.

docs.title: Token lifetimes and refresh policy
docs.text:
Status: Accepted, 2026-11-18.

Amended:

  • 2026-11-19: the migration caps each refresh token relative to its access token.
  • 2026-11-19: one session per client is now the default, and the client policy can turn it off per client.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Access tokens lasted one month and refresh tokens 100 years. Each time a new access token was issued, the RevokeOldTokens listener revoked the user's older access tokens for that client, but left their refresh tokens valid. The refresh grant checks only the refresh token's own revoked flag, so a leaked or superseded refresh token kept working for a century.

The relying parties limit what we can change. Booking and Flarum use the access token only at login, and Bookstack does not refresh. Control Center stores one token pair per user. Every night it refreshes each user whose access token has expired, even users who rarely log in, and then reads /api/user. If a single refresh fails, Control Center wipes that user's tokens.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Access tokens last 1 hour. Tokens already issued keep their one-month expiry.

Refresh tokens last 30 days. Each refresh issues a new refresh token, so the 30 days restart every time. There is no absolute cap.

By default, each user keeps one session per client. A client policy with single_session off keeps every session instead. RevokeOldTokens stays, and it now also revokes the refresh tokens that belong to the access tokens it revokes. The refresh token just issued belongs to the new access token, so it is never revoked.

A single migration ships with the change. It sets every live refresh token to expire 30 days after its access token expires, and revokes refresh tokens whose access token is already revoked. Old access tokens last up to a month after deploy, and Control Center only refreshes once its access token has expired, so a flat "deploy plus 30 days" cap could expire a refresh token before it is ever used.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Control Center renews each user's tokens on the first night after their old access token expires, and keeps them alive from then on, because 1-hour access tokens are always expired by the next nightly run. Any client that stops refreshing loses access within 30 days, and the daily passport:purge task removes the expired tokens.

A new login on one device ends the user's session with the same client on another device. No current client notices, since each keeps one token pair per user on its server.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Dropping RevokeOldTokens would allow sessions on several devices, and short-lived tokens already limit what a leak can do. We kept it because it matches today's behaviour and closes the gap directly. The client policy now lets an administrator turn it off for a client that needs sessions on several devices.

An absolute cap, such as one year, would quietly wipe Control Center tokens for users who rarely log in.

Token revocation (RFC 7009) and introspection (RFC 7662) are out of scope. No relying party asked for them.

docs.title: Client ids and schema
docs.text:
Status: Accepted, 2026-11-19.

Amended:

  • 2026-11-19: legacy columns drop after a prod beta, inside 4.0.0.
  • 2026-11-20: new clients get default allowed scopes, and a missing policy row fails closed.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: oauth_clients still has the pre-13 Passport layout: integer ids, a comma-separated redirect column, and grant types derived at runtime from two booleans. Every admin-created client is confidential and first-party, so each one silently allows implicit, client_credentials and device_code as well as authorization_code and refresh_token. Live relying parties hold integer client ids in their config, and we don't know every party that relies on today's grants.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Adopt Passport 13's layout: add redirect_uris, grant_types and owner, and backfill them. The legacy columns (user_id, redirect, personal_access_client, password_client) and the oauth_personal_access_clients table are dropped in a later PR. It merges after VATSCA's production has run a 4.0.0 beta containing the schema change, and still ships in 4.0.0. Self-hosters upgrading from 3.x backfill and drop in one migrate, and roll back by restoring their backup.

Clients keep one table with a string id. Existing clients keep their integer ids, such as "5". New clients get UUIDv7 ids (Passport::$clientUuids = true). Every client_id column becomes a string. The client model accepts digit-only keys in route binding, so admin URLs for legacy clients still resolve.

Existing clients keep exactly the grant types they have today. New clients get only authorization_code and refresh_token. Admins can change a client's grant types in the admin form.

Per-client settings that Passport does not know about live in oauth_client_policies. It has one row per client, keyed by client_id, with typed columns. Every client has a row: the backfill creates one for each existing client, and creating a client creates its row. Columns that have a sensible default get it in the database.

Allowed scopes have no database default. The backfill allows each existing client every scope that exists before the policy: full_name, email, vatsim_details, country and groups. A new client starts with the default scopes, full_name, email, vatsim_details and country. These are the scopes Passport granted by default before the policy, so a client created outside the admin form, such as with passport:client, behaves as before. The admin form requires an administrator to choose a new client's scopes, which replace the defaults.

Code treats a missing row as a fault and fails closed. The authorize endpoint refuses the sign-in, the token endpoint refuses any grant with a user, a grant without a user can get no scope, and the client keeps one session per user.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Legacy clients keep client_credentials, so Passport's guard against a user id equal to a client id (TokenGuard.php:146) still applies to them. It cannot fire in practice, because user ids are VATSIM CIDs and client ids are small.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Moving legacy clients to a separate table: Passport has a single client model and repository, and token tables can point at only one table.

Re-registering every client with a UUID: this breaks every live relying party for no security gain.

Trimming legacy grants to authorization code and refresh: this could break unknown users of the other grants. Admins can trim them one client at a time instead.

Policy columns on oauth_clients: a side table keeps our columns clear of future Passport schema changes.

Optional policy rows, where a missing row means defaults: the safe default for a missing row is to refuse the client, and the useful default for a new client is to keep Passport's old default scopes. One fallback can't serve both, so every client has a row and a missing row is a fault.

docs.title: Signing keys and rotation
docs.text:
Status: Accepted, 2026-11-19.

Amended:

  • 2026-11-20: a manifest records every key's state, the commands are named signing-keys:*, and the import removes Passport's key files.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Handover signs access tokens with one RSA keypair. The entrypoint creates it on first boot in the storage volume. Access tokens carry no kid, and nothing can rotate the key. OIDC adds id_tokens and a JWKS. vcas-ok will check access tokens against that JWKS. Other vACCs run the same image with only a volume and env vars, and have no secret store.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Keys are files in storage/oauth-keys, one private key per file, named <kid>.key. A manifest, keys.json, records each key's state, when it entered that state, and whether it was imported. One atomic write of the manifest moves a key between states, so a reader never sees two active keys. The kid is the RFC 7638 thumbprint. Keys are RS256 only. New keys are RSA 2048.

One active key signs both access tokens and id_tokens, and both carry a kid. Passport's access token entity is subclassed to add the header. Passport's resource server validator is replaced by one that picks the key by kid from every published key.

Rotation is manual, run with the signing-keys:* artisan commands. A key moves through four states: staged (published, not signing), then active, then retired (published, not signing), then removed. Activation waits until the key has been staged for 1h, the JWKS cache time. Removal waits until the key has been retired for 2h. --force overrides both waits. An emergency revoke drops a key at once and, if it was active, activates a fresh one with no staging.

signing-keys:import fills an empty store. It imports PASSPORT_PRIVATE_KEY if set, and warns that the variable is now ignored. Otherwise it imports oauth-private.key and deletes Passport's key files. On a fresh install it creates and activates a key with no staging. The container entrypoint runs it on every start, and a migration runs it once. It imports nothing once the store holds keys. Tokens with no kid are checked against the imported key while it is still published.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Rotating the RSA key never touches refresh tokens or auth codes, which are encrypted with APP_KEY. A revoked key fails its live tokens at once, and relying parties recover by refreshing. An id_token_hint signed by a removed key can't be verified.

Passport no longer reads oauth-private.key, oauth-public.key or the PASSPORT_*_KEY variables. Once the import deletes Passport's key files, rolling back to 3.x needs the storage volume backup.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Keys in a DB table encrypted with APP_KEY: losing or rotating APP_KEY would lose the signing keys too.

Keys in env vars or a secret store: a changing set of keys needs a redeploy, and other vACCs have no secret store.

A separate rotating key for id_tokens, with access tokens left on the Passport key: the Passport key could then never rotate, and access tokens would still lack a kid. Many JWKS clients reject those.

Scheduled rotation: more moving parts for a small org, and it breaks relying parties that pin a key by hand.

Commands named keys:*: keys:generate is one letter from Laravel's key:generate, which replaces APP_KEY. A passport:keys:* prefix would sit next to Passport's own passport:keys, which writes the key files Handover no longer reads.

docs.title: OAuth clients
docs.text:
An OAuth client is a service that lets members log in through Handover, such as Control Center or a forum. Each client gets an ID, which the service uses to talk to Handover. A confidential client also gets a secret.

Administrators manage clients. An administrator is a direct member of a group marked as an admin group, see groups.

docs.title: Managing clients in the browser
docs.text:
Open OAuth Clients in the header of the groups pages, or go to /admin/oauth-clients. The page lists every active client with its ID, name, redirect URIs, grant types, allowed scopes and who may sign in.

  • New client: choose the client type, enter a descriptive name and the redirect URIs of the service, and tick the scopes it may request. Members see the name, so make it clear.
  • Edit: change the name, redirect URIs, post-logout redirect URIs, grant types, allowed scopes, allowed origins, required groups or single session setting.
  • Regenerate: create a new secret for a confidential client. The old secret stops working at once.
  • Delete: remove the client and revoke its existing tokens.

Copy the secret right away

Handover stores only a hash of the secret. It shows the plaintext secret once, after you create a client or regenerate its secret. If you lose it, regenerate the secret and update the service.

A new client gets a UUID as its ID. Clients created before 4.0.0 keep their numeric ID.

docs.title: Client type
docs.text:
Choose the type when you create a client. You cannot change it later.

Type Use Confidential The service runs on a server and keeps the secret there. This is the default. Public The service runs in the member's browser, such as a single-page app, where a secret cannot be kept.

A public client has no secret and no Regenerate button. It must prove each sign-in with PKCE, using the S256 method, see public clients. It may have only the Authorization code and Refresh token grant types. The list marks it as Public.

A client created before 4.0.0 without a secret is a public client.

docs.title: Redirect URIs
docs.text:
A client can have several redirect URIs, such as one per hostname of the service. The service must send one of them exactly, so https://example.test/callback does not match https://example.test/callback/.

A public client's redirect URIs must use https. For development, http is also allowed on localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1], with any port.

docs.title: Post-logout redirect URIs
docs.text:
Post-logout redirect URIs set where Handover may send a member after the service logs them out of Handover, see logout. A client has none until you add them, and the form does not fill them in from the redirect URIs. Add them only for a service that logs members out through Handover.

They follow the same rules as the client's redirect URIs. The service must send one of them exactly.

docs.title: Grant types
docs.text:
Grant types set how a client may get tokens. A new client gets Authorization code and Refresh token, which is what a service that signs members in needs.

Grant type Use Authorization code Sign members in through the browser. Refresh token Get a new access token without signing the member in again. Untick it to make members sign in again once the access token expires. Client credentials Let the service get a token for itself, with no member.

Clients created before 4.0.0 keep the grant types they had, which include client credentials, implicit and device code. Handover does not support implicit, password, personal access or device code. The form shows them only on clients that already have them, so you can untick them but not add them. If a service does not use a grant type, untick it.

A public client may have only Authorization code and Refresh token.

docs.title: Allowed scopes
docs.text:
Allowed scopes set which scopes a client may request. A new client has none ticked, so you must tick at least one. Tick only the scopes the service needs.

If a service requests a scope that is not ticked, the sign-in fails with the invalid_scope error. If you remove a scope that a service already holds, its next token refresh fails with the invalid_scope error, and the member must sign in again. If a service requests no scopes, it gets the default scopes full_name, email, vatsim_details and country, limited to the ones that are ticked. If none of those are ticked, the service gets a token with no scopes.

Clients created in 3.x allow every scope except openid and profile. Tick those when a service moves to OpenID Connect.

docs.title: Allowed origins
docs.text:
Allowed origins set where a public client may call Handover's token and UserInfo endpoints from the browser. Confidential clients have none.

Enter each origin as a scheme, a host and an optional port, with no path, such as https://app.example.test or http://localhost:5173. Like a public client's redirect URIs, an origin must use https, or http on a loopback host for development. Handover stores each origin in the form a browser sends it: in lowercase, and without the default port 443 or 80.

When you create a public client, the form fills in the origins of its redirect URIs. Change them if the service calls Handover from another origin. A request from an origin that is not on the list fails, see public clients.

docs.title: Required groups
docs.text:
Required groups set who may sign in to a client. If you tick no groups, every member may sign in. If you tick one or more groups, only members of at least one of them may sign in. Membership includes member groups: someone in a member group of a required group may sign in too.

A member outside the required groups sees an error page in Handover that names the client. Handover does not send them back to the service.

Handover checks the groups again each time the service refreshes a token. If the member has left the required groups, the refresh fails with the invalid_grant error. Access tokens that Handover already issued stay valid until they expire, for up to one hour.

You cannot delete a group while a client requires it. Remove the group from the client first.

docs.title: Single session
docs.text:
By default, Single session is ticked, and each member can have one session with the client. When a member signs in again, Handover revokes their earlier access and refresh tokens for that client.

Untick it to let a member stay signed in to the service on several devices at once.

docs.title: Managing clients on the command line
docs.text:
You can also create a client with Passport's command:

php artisan passport:client

Answer the prompts with a descriptive name and the redirect URI of the service, and keep the client confidential. The command prints the client ID and secret. A client created this way may request the default scopes, admits every member and keeps a single session. To change that, edit the client in the browser.

To revoke a client and all its tokens, run the command below. It asks for the client ID.

php artisan passport:client:delete
Executing commands in containers

If you're using a container you need to execute the command inside of the container. For example, if you're using Docker you must prefix the command with docker exec and specify the container name. Here's an example where we assume that the container is handover:

docker exec -it --user www-data handover COMMAND [ARGUMENTS...]

docs.title: What members see
docs.text:
Members never see a consent screen. Handover approves every client automatically, because the clients belong to your division.

The dashboard lists the services a member has authorised that still hold an active token.

Next, configure the service itself, see connecting a client.

docs.title: Connecting a client
docs.text: Handover works like VATSIM Connect. A service that supports VATSIM Connect can use Handover by changing the URLs, the client ID and the secret. A service that supports OpenID Connect can use Handover's discovery, ID token and UserInfo endpoint instead. See OpenID Connect.

docs.title: OAuth credentials
docs.text:
First create an OAuth client in Handover. Then configure the service with:

Setting Value Method Authorization code Client ID The ID of the client: a number for older clients, a UUID for new ones Client secret The secret shown when you created the client. A public client has none. Authorization endpoint https://YOUR_HANDOVER/oauth/authorize Token endpoint https://YOUR_HANDOVER/oauth/token User information endpoint https://YOUR_HANDOVER/api/user JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) https://YOUR_HANDOVER/.well-known/jwks.json

The callback URL of the service must exactly match one of the client's redirect URIs in Handover.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
Request the scopes the service needs, separated by spaces. The service may request only the scopes its client allows. A request for any other scope fails with the invalid_scope error. A refresh fails the same way if an administrator removes a scope that the token holds. For details, see allowed scopes.

Scope Gives access to full_name First and last name email E-mail address vatsim_details Ratings, region, division and subdivision country Country groups The groups the member belongs to openid Sign in with OpenID Connect. The user API ignores it. profile First and last name, as OpenID Connect claims. The user API ignores it.

If the service requests no scopes, Handover grants full_name, email, vatsim_details and country, limited to the scopes the client allows. It never grants groups, openid or profile by default.

See the user API for the data each scope returns.

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text:
• An access token expires after one hour. To get a new access token, use the refresh token.
  • A refresh token expires after 30 days. Each refresh returns a new refresh token that is valid for another 30 days. Store the new refresh token, because the old one stops working.
  • By default, each member can have one session per client. When a member signs in again, Handover revokes their earlier access and refresh tokens for that client. An administrator can turn this off per client. See single session.
  • If the client has required groups, a refresh fails with the invalid_grant error once the member has left them. Send the member through the sign-in again.
  • Handover deletes revoked and expired tokens daily. For details, see background jobs.
  • Handover may replace its signing key without warning if the key leaks. Access tokens signed by that key then fail. Use the refresh token to get a new access token. See signing keys.

docs.title: Verifying access tokens
docs.text:
Most services send the access token to Handover and never read it. If the service checks access tokens itself:

  • An access token is a JWT signed with RS256. Its kid header names the signing key.
  • Pick the key by kid from the JWKS. When you see an unknown kid, fetch the JWKS again.
  • Cache the JWKS for at most one hour.
  • If the token holds the groups scope, it carries a groups claim with the IDs of the member's groups. See groups.

docs.title: Control Center
docs.text: Control Center supports Handover out of the box. See Control Center's documentation for its settings.

docs.title: OpenID Connect
docs.text: Handover is an OpenID Connect provider. A service that supports OpenID Connect can sign members in with discovery, an ID token and the UserInfo endpoint, instead of the VATSIM Connect-style user API.

docs.title: Turning on OpenID Connect for a client
docs.text:
OpenID Connect is opt-in for each client. To turn it on, tick openid in the client's allowed scopes, and usually profile, email and groups as well. Clients created in 3.x do not have openid either. A request for openid from a client that does not allow it fails with the invalid_scope error.

The service keeps its client ID, secret and redirect URIs. A service that runs in the browser needs a public client. The user API keeps working for every client.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Configure the service with the discovery URL:

https://YOUR_HANDOVER/.well-known/openid-configuration

The discovery document lists the endpoints, scopes and claims that Handover supports. The issuer is Handover's APP_URL, without a trailing slash. Services compare the issuer exactly, so set APP_URL to the public URL that services use. See environment variables.

If the service cannot read discovery, configure it with these settings instead:

Setting Value Issuer https://YOUR_HANDOVER Authorization endpoint https://YOUR_HANDOVER/oauth/authorize Token endpoint https://YOUR_HANDOVER/oauth/token UserInfo endpoint https://YOUR_HANDOVER/oauth/userinfo JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) https://YOUR_HANDOVER/.well-known/jwks.json End session endpoint https://YOUR_HANDOVER/oauth/logout Response type code Signing algorithm RS256

docs.title: Scopes and claims
docs.text:
Request openid together with the scopes for the claims the service needs. The ID token and the UserInfo endpoint return the same claims.

Scope Claims openid sub: the member's CID, as a string profile name, given_name and family_name email email groups groups: the IDs of the member's groups, see groups

Handover does not send email_verified. Some libraries refuse to link accounts by e-mail without it. Configure the service not to require it. The full_name, vatsim_details and country scopes add no claims. They apply to the user API only. Handover leaves out a claim that has no value, such as family_name for a member with no last name.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
The groups claim is an array of group IDs. Each ID is a UUID that never changes. The array covers every group the member belongs to, including groups they inherit through member groups. It is empty when the member belongs to no group.

Map roles in the service from group IDs, not from group names or slugs. Administrators can rename a group at any time, but its ID stays the same.

When the client is granted groups, the access token also carries a groups claim with the same IDs. Handover sets the list when it issues the token, so it can be up to one hour out of date.

docs.title: ID token
docs.text:
The token endpoint returns an id_token next to the access token when the sign-in grants openid. Verify its signature the same way as an access token. See verifying access tokens.

Claim Value iss The issuer sub The member's CID, as a string aud The client ID iat When Handover issued the ID token exp When the ID token expires, one hour after iat auth_time When the member signed in to Handover. Left out if the member's Handover session started before the upgrade to 4.0.0. nonce The nonce the service sent to the authorization endpoint, if it sent one at_hash The hash of the access token

Send a nonce with each sign-in and check that the ID token returns it. A refresh returns a new access token and refresh token, but no ID token.

docs.title: UserInfo endpoint
docs.text:
Send the access token to /oauth/userinfo with GET or POST. Handover returns the claims as JSON:

GET /oauth/userinfo
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN

{
  "sub": "1234567",
  "name": "Jane Doe",
  "given_name": "Jane",
  "family_name": "Doe",
  "email": "jane@example.org",
  "groups": ["0195f1d2-7c1a-7b3e-9a41-2f0c8d6e4b10"]
}

An access token without the openid scope gets a 403 response with the insufficient_scope error. A missing or invalid access token gets a 401 response.

docs.title: Public clients
docs.text:
A service that runs in the member's browser, such as a single-page app, cannot keep a secret. Register it as a public client instead. A public client has no secret, so it signs members in with the authorization code flow and PKCE (RFC 7636).

  • Send a code_challenge with code_challenge_method=S256 to the authorization endpoint. Handover refuses a request without a challenge, or with the plain method, with the invalid_request error.
  • Send the matching code_verifier and the client_id to the token endpoint, but no client_secret.
  • A refresh needs only the refresh_token and the client_id.

A public client can call the token endpoint and the UserInfo endpoint from the browser. Handover allows a call only from the client's allowed origins:

  • The token endpoint checks the Origin header against the allowed origins of the client named by client_id.
  • The UserInfo endpoint checks the Origin header against the allowed origins of the client the access token was issued to.
  • If the origin is not allowed, Handover refuses the request with a 403 response and no CORS headers.

Handover does not check the Origin header for a confidential client, and sends it no CORS headers.

Handover answers a CORS preflight for an origin that any client allows. The responses never allow credentials, so do not send cookies with these calls. The authorization endpoint and the user API do not support CORS.

Refresh tokens and sessions work for a public client as they do for a confidential one. Each refresh returns a new refresh token, and the single session setting applies. A public client often runs on several devices per member, so consider turning single session off for it.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text:
A service can log the member out of Handover when they log out of the service (OpenID Connect RP-Initiated Logout 1.0). Send the member's browser to the end session endpoint, /oauth/logout, with GET or a form POST:

GET /oauth/logout?id_token_hint=ID_TOKEN&post_logout_redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fservice.example.org%2Flogged-out&state=STATE
Parameter Use id_token_hint Optional. An ID token Handover issued to the service for the member. An expired ID token works. client_id Optional. The client ID. Send it when you send no id_token_hint. post_logout_redirect_uri Optional. Where Handover sends the member after logout. It must exactly match one of the client's post-logout redirect URIs. state Optional. Handover adds it to the post_logout_redirect_uri unchanged.

Handover ignores ui_locales and logout_hint.

Handover answers a POST with a redirect to the same endpoint with GET, because the browser does not send Handover's session cookie with a POST from another site. The parameters, including the id_token_hint, then appear in the URL.

Handover checks the id_token_hint signature against its published keys, and checks its iss. It does not check exp. If Handover cannot verify the hint, it treats the request as if it had no hint.

Handover takes the client from the aud of the hint, or from client_id. If both are present and name different clients, Handover shows an error page and does not redirect. If the post_logout_redirect_uri is not registered for that client, or Handover cannot tell the client, Handover shows an error page and does not redirect.

What happens next depends on who is signed in to Handover:

  • If the hint names the member who is signed in, Handover logs them out without asking.
  • If someone else is signed in, or the request has no valid hint, Handover asks the member to confirm the logout. If they confirm, Handover logs them out.
  • If nobody is signed in, Handover does not ask.

After logout, Handover sends the member to the post_logout_redirect_uri, with state if you sent one. Without a post_logout_redirect_uri, Handover shows a page that says the member is logged out.

Logout ends the member's session in Handover only. Handover revokes no access or refresh tokens, and the member stays signed in to VATSIM and to other services. End the member's session in the service before you send them to Handover.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Handover does not support back-channel or front-channel logout, so it does not tell other services when a member logs out.
  • Handover ignores the max_age and claims request parameters.
  • Handover never shows a consent screen and ignores prompt=consent. prompt=none and prompt=login work as OpenID Connect defines.

docs.title: VATSIM Connect
docs.text: Handover logs members in through VATSIM Connect. Your division needs its own OAuth client there.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Create an OAuth client for your division at VATSIM Connect.
  2. Set its redirect URL to /login on your Handover, for example https://handover.example.org/login.
  3. Set these environment variables:
Variable Explanation VATSIM_OAUTH_BASE Base URL of VATSIM Connect, https://auth.vatsim.net by default VATSIM_OAUTH_CLIENT The client ID from VATSIM Connect VATSIM_OAUTH_SECRET The client secret from VATSIM Connect VATSIM_OAUTH_SCOPES The scopes to request, full_name,email,vatsim_details,country by default

Members must grant all of these scopes. Handover refuses the login if VATSIM Connect does not return the e-mail address and VATSIM details.

docs.title: Who can log in
docs.text:
Handover refuses a login when the member:

  • is suspended on VATSIM (rating 0),
  • has an inactive VATSIM account (rating -1), or
  • is banned in Handover. The member sees the reason and the APP_OWNER_CONTACT address.

Handover also logs out members whose stored rating is 0.

docs.title: Keeping data up to date
docs.text: Handover stores the VATSIM Connect tokens of each member. A daily job uses them to fetch fresh data from VATSIM, see background jobs.

docs.title: User API
docs.text: Clients fetch the logged-in member's data from one endpoint, available at two paths. The response has the same shape as VATSIM Connect's, plus an optional groups array.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
GET /api/user
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
Accept: application/json

GET /api/v1/user is an alias. It returns exactly the same response.

docs.title: Response
docs.text:
{
  "status": "success",
  "data": {
    "cid": 1234567,
    "personal": {
      "name_first": "Jane",
      "name_last": "Doe",
      "name_full": "Jane Doe",
      "name_full_cid": "Jane Doe (1234567)",
      "email": "jane@example.org",
      "country": { "id": "NO", "name": "N/A" }
    },
    "vatsim": {
      "rating": { "id": 3, "short": "S2", "long": "Tower Controller" },
      "pilotrating": { "id": 0, "short": "P0", "long": "No Pilot Rating" },
      "region": { "id": "EMEA", "name": "N/A" },
      "division": { "id": "EUD", "name": "N/A" },
      "subdivision": { "id": "SCA", "name": "N/A" }
    },
    "oauth": { "token_valid": "true" },
    "groups": []
  }
}

The values above are examples.

docs.title: Fields and scopes
docs.text:
Every field is always present, except groups. A field is null when the token lacks the scope for it.

Field Scope cid none, always set personal.name_first, name_last, name_full, name_full_cid full_name personal.email email personal.country.id country vatsim.rating, pilotrating, region.id, division.id, subdivision.id vatsim_details groups groups. The key is missing without it

Notes:

  • Every name field under country, region, division and subdivision is always "N/A".
  • oauth.token_valid is always the string "true". Handover rejects invalid tokens before it builds a response.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
With the groups scope, groups lists every group the member belongs to, sorted by name. It includes groups the member inherits through member groups.

{
  "id": "018f1e2a-7c3d-7000-8000-abcdef012345",
  "slug": "vacc-norway",
  "name": "vACC Norway",
  "direct": true,
  "tags": ["vacc", "eur"],
  "attributes": {
    "region": "EUR",
    "division": "EUD"
  }
}
Field Explanation id UUIDv7. Use this as the stable reference in your service slug Human-readable name in URLs. It can change name Display name direct true for direct membership, false for inherited membership tags Free-form tags attributes Key/value pairs from the attribute definitions

Tags and attributes carry no stability promise.

Compatibility

Once groups have member groups, groups includes inherited groups. Clients that want only directly assigned groups should filter on direct: true.

docs.title: Background jobs
docs.text:
Handover relies on Laravel's scheduler for recurring work. Run the scheduler every minute from a crontab outside the container:

* * * * * docker exec --user www-data -i handover php artisan schedule:run >/dev/null

docs.title: Scheduled jobs
docs.text: Job Runs What it does member:data Daily Fetches fresh member data from VATSIM Connect passport:purge Daily Removes revoked tokens and tokens that expired more than seven days ago

docs.title: Member data
docs.text:
For every member with stored VATSIM Connect tokens, member:data:

  1. Refreshes the VATSIM Connect token if it has expired.
  2. Fetches the member from VATSIM Connect.
  3. Updates name, e-mail, ratings, country, region, division and subdivision.

If the token refresh fails, Handover deletes the stored tokens. The member's data then stays as it is until the next login.

docs.title: Artisan commands
docs.text:
Handover adds these commands to Laravel's php artisan.

Executing commands in containers

If you're using a container you need to execute the command inside of the container. For example, if you're using Docker you must prefix the command with docker exec and specify the container name. Here's an example where we assume that the container is handover:

docker exec -it --user www-data handover COMMAND [ARGUMENTS...]
Command Purpose groups:add-admin CID Add a member to the System Administrators group key:get Print the current application key member:data Fetch fresh member data from VATSIM Connect passport:client:delete Revoke an OAuth client and all its tokens reset:acceptedprivacy Make every member accept the Data Protection Policy again signing-keys:activate KID Make a staged signing key the active key signing-keys:generate Create a staged signing key signing-keys:import Import the Passport signing key, or create the first key signing-keys:list List the signing keys and their states signing-keys:remove KID Remove a retired signing key signing-keys:revoke KID Remove a signing key immediately

docs.title: groups:add-admin
docs.text:
php artisan groups:add-admin 1234567

Adds the member with the given CID to the group with the slug system-administrators. If the group does not exist, the command creates it as an admin group. The member must have logged in to Handover once.

The command fails if a group with that slug exists but is not an admin group. Fix that group by hand first.

docs.title: key:get
docs.text: Prints the application key, so you can set it as APP_KEY. See installation.

docs.title: member:data
docs.text: Updates every member who has VATSIM Connect tokens stored. The scheduler runs it daily, see background jobs.

docs.title: passport:client:delete
docs.text: Asks for a client ID and a confirmation. It then revokes the client, its access tokens and its refresh tokens. You can also delete clients in the admin pages.

docs.title: reset:acceptedprivacy
docs.text: Marks every member as not having accepted the Data Protection Policy. See updating the policy.

docs.title: Signing key commands
docs.text:
These commands manage the keys that sign access tokens. For when to run them, see signing keys.

The keys live in /app/storage/oauth-keys:

  • <kid>.key holds one private key. Only the user that runs Handover can read it.
  • keys.json records the state of each key, when it entered that state, and whether it was imported.

The kid is the RFC 7638 thumbprint of the public key. Keys use RS256.

docs.title: signing-keys:generate
docs.text:
php artisan signing-keys:generate

Creates a 2048-bit RSA key in the staged state and prints its kid. Handover publishes the key but does not sign with it.

docs.title: signing-keys:activate
docs.text:
php artisan signing-keys:activate KID

Makes a staged key the active key and retires the old active key. The command refuses until the key has been staged for one hour. --force skips the wait.

docs.title: signing-keys:remove
docs.text:
php artisan signing-keys:remove KID

Deletes a retired key and stops publishing it. The command refuses until the key has been retired for two hours. --force skips the wait.

docs.title: signing-keys:revoke
docs.text:
php artisan signing-keys:revoke KID

Deletes a key in any state, immediately. Tokens it signed stop working. If the key was active, the command creates and activates a new key, with no staging.

docs.title: signing-keys:import
docs.text:
php artisan signing-keys:import

Creates or imports the first key. The container runs it on every start, and a migration runs it once. If the key store already holds keys, the command does nothing. Otherwise it does one of the following:

  • If PASSPORT_PRIVATE_KEY is set, it imports that key as the active key.
  • If /app/storage/oauth-private.key exists, it imports that key as the active key, then deletes oauth-private.key and oauth-public.key.
  • Otherwise, it creates a new key and activates it.

An imported key keeps its size. Handover ignores PASSPORT_PRIVATE_KEY and PASSPORT_PUBLIC_KEY after the import. The command prints a warning while PASSPORT_PRIVATE_KEY is still set.

docs.title: signing-keys:list
docs.text:
php artisan signing-keys:list

Lists each key with its kid, its state, the time it entered that state, and whether it was imported.

docs.title: Passport commands
docs.text:
Laravel Passport provides these commands. Handover uses them as follows.

Command Purpose passport:client Create an OAuth client, see OAuth clients passport:keys Not used. Handover ignores the keys it creates. Use the signing key commands instead passport:hash Hash stored client secrets, needed once when upgrading to 4.0.0 passport:purge Remove revoked and expired tokens. The scheduler runs it daily

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Configure Handover through environment variables on the container. The repository's docker-compose.yaml lists the ones most installations need. Override a variable when its default does not fit.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Variable Default value Explanation APP_OWNER VATSIM Full name of your division, shown in the footer as the one who runs your Handover APP_OWNER_SHORT SCA Short name of your division, usually 3 letters, shown to banned users APP_OWNER_CONTACT webmaster@vatsim.net E-mail address members contact for help. Shown on error pages, and to banned users to dispute a ban APP_DPP_URL https://vatsim.net URL to your full Data Protection Policy APP_DPP_DATE 2019-10-10 Date of your Data Protection Policy, shown as free text APP_DPO_MAIL webmaster@vatsim.net E-mail address of your Data Protection Officer APP_URL http://localhost Public URL of your Handover APP_ENV production Environment of your Handover APP_KEY none Application key, see installation DB_CONNECTION mysql Database connection type DB_HOST 127.0.0.1 Database host DB_PORT 3306 Database port DB_DATABASE handover Database name DB_USERNAME root Database username DB_PASSWORD root Database password DB_TABLE_PREFIX empty Prefix for all database table names VATSIM_OAUTH_BASE https://auth.vatsim.net Base URL of VATSIM Connect VATSIM_OAUTH_CLIENT none OAuth client ID of your division at VATSIM Connect VATSIM_OAUTH_SECRET none OAuth client secret of your division at VATSIM Connect

docs.title: Optional: Theming
docs.text:
See customising the theme for how to apply these.

Variable Default value Explanation APP_LOGO vatsca.svg File name of your logo in /app/public/images/logos APP_TAGLINE Centralised Login Service Short description shown beneath the name on the front page

docs.title: Optional: Extras
docs.text: Variable Default value Explanation APP_DEBUG false Show detailed error pages. Never enable in production APP_OWNER_SUPPORT none HTML telling members where to get help, shown on the 403, 500 and 503 error pages instead of the line pointing to APP_OWNER_CONTACT. See support on error pages VATSIM_OAUTH_SCOPES full_name,email,vatsim_details,country Comma-separated scopes Handover requests from VATSIM Connect SESSION_LIFETIME 360 Session lifetime in minutes. Users must log in again when it passes SENTRY_LARAVEL_DSN none The Sentry DSN. Falls back to SENTRY_DSN SENTRY_TRACES_SAMPLE_RATE 0.0 The Sentry traces sample rate

docs.title: Support on error pages
docs.text:
Error pages for 403, 500 and 503 end with a line telling members where to get help. By default it points to APP_OWNER_CONTACT. Set APP_OWNER_SUPPORT to replace it with your own HTML, for example a link to your helpdesk or Discord:

environment:
  - 'APP_OWNER_SUPPORT=Ask for help in <a href="https://discord.gg/example">#support on our Discord</a>.'

Handover shows the HTML as it is, without escaping, so only put HTML you trust here.

docs.title: Custom container image
docs.text:
Depending on the changes you'd like to make, you may choose to create a variant of Handover based on the upstream version.

Warning

Creating a custom variant is limited to people with prior development experience. We recommend that most, if not all, users should use the standard container image.

This is the most reliable way to make changes over time, as well as regularly synchronise the changes with the upstream.

docs.title: Custom image
docs.text:
Custom derivation of Handover
FROM ghcr.io/vatsim-scandinavia/handover:v4

# Make your customisations here
...

Tip

The v4 tag follows the latest release of that major version. Pin an exact tag, such as 4.0.0-beta.7, if you'd rather decide for yourself when to pick up a new release.

docs.title: Custom theme
docs.text:
You can customise the theme by creating a _custom.scss override and running container/theme/build.sh to recompile the assets:

Custom theme in Handover
FROM ghcr.io/vatsim-scandinavia/handover:v4

# Copy your theme override
COPY _custom.scss /app/resources/sass/themes/_custom.scss

# Make the theme build script executable and run it
RUN chmod +x container/theme/build.sh && container/theme/build.sh

docs.title: Data protection policy
docs.text: Handover stores member data only after the member accepts your Data Protection Policy (DPP).

docs.title: How members accept the policy
docs.text:
When a member logs in for the first time, Handover shows a summary of your policy with a link to the full text. Handover creates the account only when the member accepts. Members who accepted before skip this step.

Configure the policy with these environment variables:

  • APP_DPP_URL links to the full policy.
  • APP_DPP_DATE shows when you last updated it.
  • APP_DPO_MAIL is where members ask to have their data deleted.

To change the summary itself, see simplified Data Protection Policy.

docs.title: Updating the policy
docs.text:
When you update the policy, make every member accept it again:

  1. Update APP_DPP_URL and APP_DPP_DATE.
  2. If needed, update the simplified version.

  3. Reset the acceptance for all users:

    docker exec -it --user www-data handover php artisan reset:acceptedprivacy

  4. Delete all sessions, so everyone must log in again:

    docker exec -it --user www-data handover sh -c 'rm -rf /app/storage/framework/sessions/*'

docs.title: Signing keys
docs.text:
Handover signs every access token with an RSA key. Services check the signature against the public keys that Handover publishes. This page explains how to rotate a key, and how to replace one that has leaked.

Executing commands in containers

If you're using a container you need to execute the command inside of the container. For example, if you're using Docker you must prefix the command with docker exec and specify the container name. Here's an example where we assume that the container is handover:

docker exec -it --user www-data handover COMMAND [ARGUMENTS...]

docs.title: Back up the keys
docs.text:
Handover keeps its keys on the storage volume, in /app/storage/oauth-keys. Back up the storage volume. If you lose the keys, every access token stops working until the service refreshes it.

On the first start, the container creates a key, or imports the key from Handover 3.x. For details, see signing-keys:import.

Always mount the storage volume

If the container starts without your storage volume, it finds no key and creates a new one. Tokens signed by your real key then fail until you mount the volume again.

docs.title: Key states
docs.text:
A key moves through these states:

State Published Signs new tokens Staged Yes No Active Yes Yes Retired Yes No Removed No No

Exactly one key is active. Handover publishes every staged, active and retired key at /.well-known/jwks.json. Services may cache the published keys for up to one hour. Handover accepts an access token only while its key is published.

To see the keys and their states, run:

php artisan signing-keys:list

docs.title: Rotate the signing key
docs.text:
Rotate the key from time to time, or when someone who had access to the storage volume leaves. No scheduled job does it for you. A rotation takes about three hours, but members and services notice nothing.

  1. Create a staged key:

    php artisan signing-keys:generate

    The command prints the kid (key ID) of the new key. Handover now publishes the key, but does not sign with it.

  2. Wait at least one hour, so every service that caches the published keys has fetched the new key.

  3. Activate the new key:

    php artisan signing-keys:activate NEW_KID

    New tokens now carry the new kid. The old key is retired: Handover still publishes it, so tokens it signed keep working.

  4. Wait at least two hours, so every access token the old key signed has expired.

  5. Remove the old key:

    php artisan signing-keys:remove OLD_KID

The commands refuse to run before the wait is over. To skip the wait, add --force. Use it only on a test system, or if you know that no service caches the published keys. A service that has not fetched the new key rejects tokens signed with it until it fetches the keys again.

The first key after an upgrade from 3.x

Access tokens from Handover 3.x last one month and have no kid. Handover checks them against the key it imported from 3.x. signing-keys:list shows that key with yes in the Imported column. Wait one month after the upgrade before you remove it, or those tokens fail and services must refresh them.

docs.title: Replace a leaked key
docs.text:
If a private key may have leaked, revoke it immediately:

php artisan signing-keys:revoke KID
  • Handover deletes the key and stops publishing it. Every access token that the key signed fails.
  • If the key was active, Handover creates a new key and activates it immediately, with no staging.
  • Services recover by using their refresh token to get a new access token. Refresh tokens do not depend on the signing key.
  • Members stay signed in to Handover.

A service that cached the published keys rejects new tokens until it fetches the keys again, which takes up to one hour. Most libraries fetch the keys again as soon as they see an unknown kid.

docs.title: Restore a backup
docs.text: The keys in /app/storage/oauth-keys must match the tokens that services hold. If you restore an older storage volume, keys created since that backup are gone, and the tokens they signed fail. Services recover by refreshing their tokens.

docs.title: Customising the theme
docs.text: You can change the logo, the colours, the front page heading, and the simplified Data Protection Policy.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
Handover ships a light and a dark theme. By default it follows the operating system. A signed-in member can switch between system, light and dark with the toggle next to their name. The choice is kept in the browser only, so it does not follow the member to another device.

Both themes are built from the same set of CSS custom properties, so anything you override below applies in either mode.

docs.title: Logo
docs.text: Bind your logo files to /app/public/images/logos and set APP_LOGO to the file name.

docs.title: Colours
docs.text: To brand your instance, put your overrides in resources/sass/themes/_custom.scss. That file is git-ignored, so your styles stay out of version control while still compiling into the regular front-end build.

docs.title: 1. Create the override file
docs.text:
Copy the example to get started:

cp resources/sass/themes/_custom.scss.example resources/sass/themes/_custom.scss

docs.title: 2. Edit your colours
docs.text:
Edit resources/sass/themes/_custom.scss. Override only what you need. Anything left out keeps its default.

Reference for the available values:

  • resources/sass/themes/_light.scss: CSS custom properties for the light theme
  • resources/sass/themes/_dark.scss: CSS custom properties for the dark theme

docs.title: 3. Rebuild the assets
docs.text:
The CSS is compiled ahead of time, so the override only takes effect once the front-end is rebuilt. How you do that depends on how you run Handover.

Without a containerWith a container 
npm run build

Build your own image with the override baked in. See custom container image.

Don't build inside a running container

The published image contains no Node toolchain, and anything compiled into a running container is lost the moment it is recreated. Either bake the theme into an image you build yourself, or run Handover without a container.

docs.title: Front page heading
docs.text:
The front page heading always says Handover. Set APP_TAGLINE to describe your instance beneath it.

The footer says your Handover is run by APP_OWNER, and credits Handover to VATSIM Scandinavia. The Handover version shows on the management pages only.

To change more than the text, bind your own Blade file to /app/resources/views/layouts/header.blade.php. Start from a copy of the original file and edit it.

docs.title: Simplified Data Protection Policy
docs.text: Before a member's data is stored, Handover shows a short summary of your Data Protection Policy as icons and bullet points. To change it, bind your own Blade file to /app/resources/views/parts/dpp-bullets.blade.php. Start from a copy of the original file and edit it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: If the colours don't change, rebuild the assets and reload the page without the cache. Check that you set each colour in both the light and the dark block of _custom.scss, so it applies in either mode.
